1971 Dodge Super Bee Barn Find Emerges With Rare Factory Feature
17 photos
Photo: Craiglist
In 1966, Dodge debuted the first-generation Charger , the first Hemi-powered Mopar. The Charger was the brand's second B-body intermediate, joining the Coronet. Two years later, Dodge added a third model to the lineup, the Super Bee. The company's affordable muscle car, it debuted alongside the Plymouth Road Runner.
While the latter was quite successful, moving over 120,000 units in its first two years on the market, the Super Bee moved significantly fewer cars. Sales peaked at 27,800 units in 1969, but Dodge delivered only 56,202 examples between 1968 and 1971. The final-year version is the rarest of the bunch, with only 5,054 made.
Like most golden-era Mopars, the 1971 Super Bee is the most sought-after in its Hemi configuration. This one is also rare, with only 22 produced. The 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) V8 vehicles are also scarce. Dodge sold only 26 equipped with the four-barrel mill and just 99 with the Six-Pack setup.
The 340-cubic-inch (5.6-liter) small-block V8, which was offered for the first time in the Super Bee in 1971, found its way into only 307 examples. This leaves us with 3,858 cars equipped with the standard 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter) V8 engine.
These Super Bees aren't particularly desirable, especially when they re-emerge into the light after decades of improper storage. The red example you see here is one of those 383-equipped models, but it's also rare thanks to a drivetrain component you don't see very often. I'm talking about the transmission.
Most 383-equipped Super Bees were born with the three-speed TorqueFlite automatic; records indicate 2,889 units. The four-speed manual version is notably rarer, as only 766 were ordered with the three-pedal layout. Well, this Mopar doesn't have that either; the original owner went with the basic configuration by pairing the 383-cubic-inch V8 with the three-speed manual transmission.
The latter was standard with the said powerplant, but most customers opted to upgrade to the four-speed or the TorqueFlite. Apparently, this Super Bee is one of only 203 examples ordered with this drivetrain combo. It's also one of far fewer units that are still around. The 1971 Super Bee Registry, which includes about 750 cars, lists only 18 vehicles with the three-speed automatic. This one would be the 19th.
The Mopar surfaced in Talladega, Alabama, and it looks like it has been off the road for a very long time. There's not much info to run by, but it was probably retired decades ago. Fortunately, the coupe is still in one piece, with not much rust to write home about. The paint could be original, but it's heavily weathered.
The interior appears to be complete, and it's actually in pretty good shape, but it needs a thorough cleaning. The floor pans need some work, as does the trunk pan. The car is missing the hood, and the right-side front fender is a bit crusty.
Sadly, the original engine is missing, with no info on what might have happened. The good news is that 383-cubic-inch V8s aren't difficult to source, with plenty of period-correct units likely out there. But the best news in this department is that the three-speed manual is still with the car. It's sitting in the trunk for now, but it can be restored.
The seller says that the Super Bee has two fender tags, indicating that it's probably a highly optioned car. Unfortunately, he did not include images of the plates, so the options list remains a mystery.
All told, this Super Bee is a pretty solid project car that will morph into a rare collectible. Not quite as desirable as a Hemi, but rare nevertheless. If you've been looking for a three-speed manual Mopar, this Super Bee is available for $12,500 .
